E0466.summary: The name given to chemical affinity, which a reader records as ruled by the three principles.
E0466.body: The text identifies it with chemical affinity: “chemical affinity, called Elective Attraction” [II.1 ¶19]. The reader's record adds that this affinity is ruled by the three principles; the voice of the passage is unclear.

E0467.summary: Ordinary, sensible fire, which Atwood distinguishes from true fire as a mere effect of an antecedent potency.
E0467.body: Atwood sets true fire apart from the fire of common experience, “distinct from that elementary ignition with which we are sensibly familiar” [I.2 ¶15]. Per the reader's record, such ignition is not true fire but only an excitation or effect of the antecedent potency [I.2 ¶15].

E0468.summary: The world over which the regenerate soul gains rule and through which it can pass.
E0468.body: Atwood speaks of the soul attaining a state “wherein it can rule over the elementary world and pass through it” [IV.4 ¶20]. The context suggests the regenerate soul is meant.

E0469.summary: In Hermetic usage not common elements or chemical simples, but properties of the universal spirit in the Mercury; the true element is a spirit of life.
E0469.body:
**Atwood's definition.** The elements of the adepts are not bodily substances: “We must not limit, says Paracelsus, an element to a bodily substance or quality” [I.2 ¶26]. Rather, “the elements they speak of, as being introverted and transformed are the elements of the Mercury, properties of the universal spirit”, and “the true element is a spirit of life, and grows in all things” [I.2 ¶26]; the visible is only its receptacle. Water, air, earth and gold are not true elements; of Nature she writes “but Her, the true element, they have never found” [III.3 ¶65], i.e. the chemists. In verse she cites, the four are divided from a first mass: “And from that lump divided I foure sundry elements,” [III.3 ¶76]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Alchemists refer to the four elements of the Universal Ether” [APP ¶69].

**Quoted authorities.** Hermes says the elements are to be taken “not corporally but spiritually and wisely” [I.3 n4]; Atwood glosses: “The philosophic water then, being divided into four parts or hypostatic relations, they are called elements” [I.3 n5]. The author of The Triumph and the Master speak of their conversion and dissolution: “you must make the conversion of the Elements” [IV.2 ¶6]; “O blessed watery Form! That dissolveth the Elements!” [IV.2 ¶14]. Eudoxus describes the Second Key, which separates the Stone's constituents and converts them in sequence: it “makes Water of Earth, Air of Water, and Fire of Air” [IV.3 ¶5].

**Identities asserted:** elements of the Mercury / properties of the universal spirit; spirit of life [I.2 ¶26]; four parts or hypostatic relations of the philosophic water [I.3 n5]; Nature (“Her”) as the true element [III.3 ¶65]; four elements of the Universal Ether [APP ¶69].

E0470.summary: Accounts of the Eleusian Mysteries, cited by Atwood in support of Wisdom as the offspring of a vital experiment into nature.
E0470.body: Atwood invokes accounts of the Eleusian Mysteries to support her view that Wisdom is the offspring of a vital experiment into nature [II.1 ¶52].

E0471.summary: A figure the Adepts declare already born: a forerunner baptizing with water, foreshowing all things to the wise, born miraculously and before the Divine Light.
E0471.body: Atwood reports the saying of the Adepts: “Natus est jam Elias Artista (5); Elias, the artist, is born already” [IV.2 ¶12] (the book's own translation). In the same passage, per the reader's record, he is described as a forerunner who baptizes with water, foreshows all things to the wise, and is born miraculously and prior to the Divine Light [IV.2 ¶12]. The voice is that of the Adepts as quoted.

E0472.summary: A spirit said in the Table Talk to be born when the metal bond is broken, whose work is to prepare for something higher.
E0472.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says that when the metal bond is broken “the Elias spirit is born and his work is to prepare for something higher.” [APP ¶139]

E0473.summary: The healing, life-prolonging and transmuting product of the Art, named in many reports of adepts and in quoted verse; also used of the soul's immortal fortification.
E0473.body:
**Reports of adepts (Atwood).** Artephius, “by the use of the elixir, is reported to have lived throughout the period of a thousand years” [I.1 ¶36]; the phrase “elixir of life” also appears in a quotation in that paragraph. “Alain de l’Isle is said to have obtained the Elixir” [I.1 ¶45]. Paracelsus is mentioned with “the elixir he boasts” [I.1 ¶64], in a sentence about “one who was in the habit of taking a potent spiritual medicine” whose effects worsened with depravity [I.1 ¶64]. Of Seton, “a report was spread about of the Elixir” [I.1 ¶66], in a passage that also speaks of the medicine he gave the sick; Starkey speaks of “the White and Red elixir” [I.1 ¶73]. Vaughan reportedly died “from an overdose of the elixir” [I.1 ¶74]. These records suggest a product that can be taken and that both heals and transmutes, though the passages do not define it.

**Quoted authorities.** Ripley: the separated elements of Mercury, “again commixed by equal weight or proportion, make the elixir complete” [I.2 ¶25]; the purged stone becomes “in whytenes Elixir of great might” [III.1 ¶62]. Bloomfield lists it among names of the privy quintessence: “Our great Elixir most high of price, Our Azot, our Basiliske, and our Adrop, our Cockatrice.” [I.2 ¶41]. Norton: “In this wise Elixir, of whom ye make mencion, Is engendered a thing of Second Intention” [IV.2 ¶34], i.e. engendered when celestial and elemental virtues accord.

**Atwood's spiritual use.** The soul, re-entering the body through death, fortifies it “with the elixir of an immortal life” [II.3 ¶39].

**Identities asserted:** Azot, Basiliske, Adrop, Cockatrice and other names (Bloomfield) [I.2 ¶41]; a thing of Second Intention (Norton) [IV.2 ¶34].

E0474.summary: Intermediate fruits of the Vital Experiment, called vital products, whose exhibition without disclosure of source astonished common chemistry.
E0474.body: Atwood treats elixir and gold together as intermediate fruits of the Vital Experiment: “Both of which are vital products” [II.4 ¶58]. Exhibited without discovery of their source, they caused much astonishment to common chemistry [II.4 ¶58].

E0475.summary: Light set free from the central essence, said to prolong life and cure disease and moral and physical defects.
E0475.body: Atwood: “This is the elixir of Light from the central essence” [I.3 n18]. In the same note it is identified with the tincture of many dyes and with the union of the purified spirit with its course, and is said to prolong life and to cure disease and moral and physical defects [I.3 n18].

E0476.summary: A condition of being beyond corporeal life and generation, the place of the third, intellectual vision and the goal of the hidden labours.
E0476.body:
For Atwood, Elysium is a state transcending corporeal life and generation, the goal of the hidden labours, and the place of the third, intellectual vision: “this third vision of the light is in Elysium” [II.4 ¶15].

**Identities asserted:** the Islands of the Blessed — “is denominated the Islands of the Blessed; and these are the same with the Elysian Fields” [II.4 ¶3]; the enclosed garden of Solomon and the Terrestrial Paradise — “This is Elysium, the enclosed garden of Solomon, where God condescends to walk and drink of the sealed fountain; the true Terrestrial Paradise” [II.4 ¶9].

E0477.summary: The light reached after passing through the dark region; the object of inquiry and the state into which the liberated soul passes.
E0477.body: Atwood says the dark region must be traversed “before inquiry can hope to meet its object in the Elysian light” [II.3 ¶5]. It is the state into which the liberated soul passes; she illustrates with Aeneas “going forth to meet his father in the Elysian fields” [II.4 ¶21], where he receives the Epopteia. See also Elysian Fields.

E0478.summary: The doctrine by which the physical universe proceeds from the superstantial Light or will and is extended and corporified by multiplication of the unit.
E0478.body:
Atwood presents an essential emanation as Kabalistic doctrine: “according to the doctrine of an essential emanation, the whole physical universe is extended and corporified” [III.2 ¶3], through multiplication of the indeficient unit into its parts under the Law of its own proceeding Light [III.2 ¶3]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) she speaks of “emanation from the superstantial Light or will” and says “The darkness is the emanation” [APP ¶66], the flat and qualitated becoming cubic by multiplication into itself [APP ¶66].

**Identity asserted:** darkness [APP ¶66].

E0479.summary: Author of Wuthering Heights, criticized in the Table Talk as a Saturnine mass of power lacking the clearing Jupiter element.
E0479.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Wuthering Heights is criticized as a Saturnine mass of power in potentiality, wanting the clearing Jupiter element; Emily is called Saturn [APP ¶175].

E0480.summary: A mid-point between mind and matter, by which mind is moved into matter.
E0480.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says: “Emotion is a mid-point between the two” [APP ¶80], i.e. between mind and matter, mind being moved into matter by it.

E0481.summary: Cited by Atwood, mainly from his Physics, in support of the soul's exile from the light, concealed harmony manifested by ether, and the twofold order of union and strife.
E0481.body: Atwood cites Empedocles approvingly on several points. On our desertion of the best life by turning to externals: “Heaven’s exiles straying from the orb of light.” [II.4 ¶9, II.4 ¶10]. From the Physics, called “a poet”, he illustrates a concealed harmony made manifest by the motion of ether: “Then all the members of the god appeared” [II.4 ¶26–28, II.4 n16]. He also serves as an instance of “the physiologist” who substitutes elements as principles, differing from others in expression only [III.2 ¶33, III.2 ¶34]. From Physics, cap. 1, she draws support for a twofold intelligible and sensible order, perpetual interchange, and the One formed from the many: “All things in union now thro’ love conspire, And now thro’ strife divulsed are borne along” [III.2 ¶38, III.2 ¶39, III.2 n35].

E0482.summary: Used pejoratively of knowledge lacking the experience, gained only by observing remote effects.
E0482.body: Atwood: “All our knowledge without the experience is empirical, the result only of observation of remote effects” [IV.4 ¶12].

E0483.summary: Something Hermes says is made from the golden matter; not explained in the text.
E0483.body: Hermes, quoted: “of them we make the encaustic of which we have written” [I.3 ¶59]; the reference is apparently to the golden matter. The text does not explain the term.

E0484.summary: The handling of the work, which has particular turnings in which Eirenaeus says he often erred.
E0484.body: Eirenaeus, quoted: “in some particular turnings of the Encheiresis I erred often” [IV.1 ¶17]. The context suggests it means the manual handling or conduct of the work.

E0485.summary: A visionary criticized in the Table Talk for lacking education of the intellect and so having little gauge for truth.
E0485.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Engelbrecht is criticized as a visionary without education of the intellect, with little gauge for truth, who perhaps misconceived the Evester [APP ¶105].

E0486.summary: The veiled teaching and its hidden meaning, whose solution comes through desire and labour and opens the mystery of all things.
E0486.body: The first class of prayer is described as “seeking a clue whereby it may enter the intelligible profundity of the Enigma” [III.4 ¶24]. Its solution arises from labour and desire, even from attempts “which were not the solution of the Enigma, the solution itself arose” [III.4 ¶22]; unfolding it opens the mystery of all things. The voice of these passages is unclear in the records.

E0487.summary: A work cited by Atwood as celebrating the Laelia Aelia as comprehending all.
E0487.body: Atwood cites the Enigma as celebrating the Laelia Aelia as comprehending all [I.2 ¶34].

E0488.summary: The riddle whose solution is to penetrate rationally the darkened essence of one's natural understanding; Mind is its Key.
E0488.body:
Atwood glosses the riddle plainly: “to solve the Enigma of the Sphinx; in other words, to penetrate rationally the darkened essence of his natural understanding” [IV.1 ¶48]. And: “For Mind is the Key of this Hermetic Enigma” [IV.1 ¶48].

**Identity asserted:** the darkened essence of one's natural understanding, to be penetrated rationally [IV.1 ¶48].

E0489.summary: A work in Ashmole's Theatrum, cited in support of Nature and Art as parents and a twofold yet indivisible work.
E0489.body: Atwood cites the Enigma Philosophicum (Ashmole’s Theatrum, p. 423) in support of Nature and Art as parents of the work, a twofold yet indivisible work, and the fixed fixing the unfixed: “There is no sun but which is twice begot” [III.3 ¶36, III.3 n24].

E0490.summary: An entity; in the Table Talk, such an ens is said to underlie the philosophic stone and to be the final term to which the sensual medium is brought.
E0490.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says “such an ens was the basis of the philosophic stone” [APP ¶108], and speaks of the sensual medium “brought to its pivot, to its last ens” [APP ¶110].

E0491.summary: An entity of light, the purer conscious ens carried back to God; named with the rejected Corner Stone as what the wise raise.
E0491.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood speaks of “the purer conscious ens of light” [APP ¶78] carried back to God, and per the reader's record relates it to the excruciated Philosophic Matter and the real Stone [APP ¶78]. In the main text the wise “raise their rejected Corner Stone and Ens of Light” [II.1 ¶8] in the living temple; it is not separately defined there.

E0492.summary: The state of being agitated by the inspiring influence of divinity, contrary to phantasy; distinguished by the ancients from fanaticism.
E0492.body: Olympiodorus, quoted: “when we are agitated by the inspiring influence of divinity, and the phantasy intervenes, the enthusiastic energy ceases” [II.2 ¶12]. Atwood notes the ancients drew a line “between enthusiasm and fanaticism” [II.4 ¶29], parallel to that between imaginative vision and the light of the true gods; she does not otherwise define it.

E0493.summary: The person in trance, susceptible to imaginative impressions that linger in a place.
E0493.body: Atwood: “the entranced Subject is more or less susceptible of all imaginative impressures” [III.4 ¶42], including, per the reader's record, those lingering in the place.

E0494.summary: Said of philosophers in a special sense: they withhold the truth only from the ignorant and vicious, not from the just or wise.
E0494.body: Hermes, quoted, explains why philosophers withhold truth only from fools and the vicious, not from the just or wise: “For this reason are philosophers said to be envious” [I.3 ¶11]; again, “For this reason are the philosophers said to be envious” [III.4 ¶9].

E0495.summary: Cited by Atwood in support of the view that the Mysteries become venerable when believed to be provided for the perfection of human life.
E0495.body: Atwood cites Epictetus in support: the Mysteries become venerable when one believes they were provided for the perfection of human life [II.4 ¶57].
